title: Engineering Graphics
tagline: Sketching, orthographic and pictorial projection, sections, dimensioning, tolerances and geometric tolerancing, and parametric CAD
summary: Engineering drawings are the language in which designs are specified, made and inspected. The course covers freehand sketching and pictorial views, orthographic projection, sectional and auxiliary views, dimensioning, tolerances and fits, geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, and parametric 3D CAD models, assemblies and working drawings.
overview: An engineering drawing is a legal instrument disguised as a picture. It is the only document that tells a machinist what to make, an inspector what to measure, a fitter what to assemble and a lawyer what was promised — and it does all four with a notation system that was settled, in its essentials, between 1901 and 1962 and has not been improved on since.

This course teaches that notation as a language: its grammar (the projection, the section, the line types), its vocabulary (the dimension, the tolerance zone, the datum) and its idiom (the conventions that exist because somebody machined a part from a misread drawing). Every rule is justified by the failure it prevents and priced in the money it saves, because a drawing is the cheapest place in engineering to be wrong and the most expensive place to have been wrong cheaply.

The course then carries the notation into the machine: the ISO tolerance system and the statistics of a fit, geometric dimensioning and tolerancing and the datum reference frame, and the parametric CAD model with its constraints, its configurations and its model-based definition. The recurring theme is the difference between the model and the part — the model is exact and nominal, the part is toleranced, and the whole of product definition is the art of saying which differences matter.

No prior drawing experience is assumed and no calculus is used beyond arithmetic and the occasional square root. What is assumed is a willingness to read a drawing closely enough to find the one dimension that contradicts another, which is the skill the course is actually about.
outcomes: Sketch and read freehand and instrument drawings, and choose the view set that describes a part without a hidden line in excess
Construct first- and third-angle projections, auxiliary views and the full family of sections, and apply the hatching and fastener conventions of an assembly section
Dimension a part once and only once, choose between chain, baseline and ordinate schemes, and predict the tolerance that each accumulates
Specify ISO 286 limits, fundamental deviations and preferred fits, compute clearance and interference ranges, and analyse a tolerance stack statistically and at worst case
Apply geometric dimensioning and tolerancing: build a datum reference frame, choose the tolerance zone shape, use maximum-material bonus and projected zones, and derive the fastener formulas
Build a parametric, fully constrained, change-tolerant CAD model, and exchange it as STEP AP242 rather than as a tessellated picture
Produce a complete working drawing set — details, assembly, envelope, schematic and parts list — that a shop can make from and a purchasing department can buy from

chapters.title: Sketching and pictorial views
chapters.summary: Freehand sketching, line types, and isometric, oblique and perspective views of objects.

chapters.title: Orthographic projection
chapters.summary: First- and third-angle projection, choosing and arranging views, and reading multiview drawings.

chapters.title: Sections and auxiliary views
chapters.summary: Full, half, offset and removed sections, hatching conventions, and auxiliary views of inclined surfaces.

chapters.title: Dimensioning
chapters.summary: Standard practice for dimensions and notes, and the dimensioning of holes, threads, chamfers and fillets.

chapters.title: Tolerances and fits
chapters.summary: Limits and tolerances, standard fits between mating parts, tolerance stack-up and surface finish.

chapters.title: Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing
chapters.summary: Datums, feature control frames, and tolerances of form, orientation, location and run-out.

chapters.title: Parametric CAD modelling
chapters.summary: Sketches, constraints and features in parametric solid modelling, and capturing design intent.

chapters.title: Assemblies and working drawings
chapters.summary: Assembly models and mating constraints, bills of materials, exploded views and production drawings.

history.title: Monge's Géométrie descriptive
history.detail: Gaspard Monge's lecture notes of 1795 gave descriptive geometry its two-plane theory of projection and with it the theoretical basis of every multiview drawing since. Monge wrote it for the École Normale and the French revolutionary government initially suppressed it as a military secret.

history.title: The first general-terms drawing standard
history.detail: The British Standards Committee's provisional specification for general-purpose engineering drawings fixed the line types, the section hatch at 45 degrees and the rule that a drawing is never scaled from — the practical motive being that a rolled drawing had to be legible at arm's length through a gap in a bundle.

history.title: Taylor's gauging address
history.detail: Charles Le Maistre Taylor's address to the Institution of Mechanical Engineers on the gauging of limit work established that a go gauge must check every feature at once and a no-go gauge only one, which is the founding proposition of dimensional metrology and the reason a plug gauge and a micrometer are not interchangeable instruments.

history.title: True position and the maximum-material bonus
history.detail: Parker and Fessler's SAE papers proposed tolerancing a feature's position to a cylindrical zone about a theoretically exact position, with bonus tolerance at maximum material condition. The idea became ANSI Y14.5 and then the geometric tolerancing of ISO 1101.
history.people: Stanley H. Parker, James E. Fessler

history.title: The history tree
history.detail: Pro/ENGINEER made constraint-based, history-based, associative modelling the industry default, so that a model recorded how a part was intended to be built and not only what it looked like. Every parametric system since descends from that decision.

history.title: The first drawingless airliner
history.detail: The Boeing 777 was defined entirely in a digital model with no drawing issued to manufacture, which forced the standardisation of model-based definition and, two decades later, of the PMI carriage in STEP AP242.
